text: Support hardware cursor and overlay planes, direct scanout, and tearing/immediate presentation for fullscreen games and HDR video.
Support hybrid-graphics laptops (iGPU plus dGPU, render offload, mux switching) across the compositor and both personalities.
Support DisplayPort MST and daisy-chained docks in the multi-monitor hot-plug test.
Adopt an ADR on proprietary GPU kernel drivers (NVIDIA proprietary module versus open kernel modules, Nouveau and NVK) covering GPL-only symbol exposure, tainting and support commitments.
rationale: GPU support is the hardest hardware blocker and the licensing posture determines which path is even possible.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Provide a software-rendered and virtio-gpu compositor path so the desktop stack can be tested headlessly in QEMU, with golden-image comparison tolerant of documented rasterisation differences.
rationale: Without a GPU-less rendering path every UI change needs physical hardware and desktop testing becomes a bottleneck.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Implement a compositor-owned lock screen that inhibits all input to applications, hides notification content by policy, locks on idle, lid close and suspend, and cannot be drawn over by any application surface.
rationale: A lock screen is table stakes for a laptop OS and must be enforced by the compositor rather than being an ordinary window.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Guarantee that a compositor crash while locked restarts into the locked state, so §32 recovery never exposes the desktop.
rationale: Compositor-restart recovery is a baseline feature, and crash-to-unlock is a well-known real-world lock screen bypass class.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Render permission prompts, file choosers and the elevation dialog through a privileged trusted-UI component in compositor-protected surfaces that applications cannot overlay, spoof, resize or synthesise input into.
rationale: A chooser that grants authority (§25) is only as strong as the guarantee that the user, not the application, drove it.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Show non-suppressible shell indicators whenever camera, microphone, screen capture or location capabilities are actively exercised, attributing use to the specific application.
rationale: Users expect these indicators from every modern OS and they make capability use visible rather than theoretical.

text: OS-owned screenshot and screen-recording tools using the compositor's capture capability, with region selection, annotation, and per-app screen-share picker for compat portals.
rationale: §40 forbids unrestricted capture so the OS itself must supply the tools users would otherwise install.

text: Colour management in the compositor: ICC profile per display, colour-managed surfaces, HDR-to-SDR tone mapping, and a night-light mode.
rationale: HDR support in §40 is incorrect without colour management and creative users will not adopt a desktop that mis-renders colour.

text: Decide whether RDP and VNC clients and a remote-desktop server built on remote surfaces are in scope for 1.0.
rationale: Remote access to Windows machines and headless boxes is how many technical users bridge a partial migration.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Spike exposing Mesa/Vulkan to a native component through Surface and Buffer capabilities without ambient /dev/dri access, and decide the GPU userspace strategy from the result.
rationale: GPU is the hardest blocker, and the native graphics abstraction is unproven until a real driver stack works behind it.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the NVIDIA support stance for 1.0 (open kernel modules with NVK/Mesa, proprietary userspace via compatibility, or unsupported) after evaluating each against the capability model.
rationale: Proprietary userspace drivers assume ambient device access and may be impossible to fit behind capabilities.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the compositor process architecture (monolithic vs split display/scene/input components) by prototyping crash-and-rebind and measuring input-to-photon latency of each.
rationale: Crash recovery and latency requirements pull in opposite directions and the split cannot be changed after the UI protocol depends on it.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide that explicit GPU synchronization (timeline semaphores / drm_syncobj) is mandatory for all native surfaces from the first compositor, with no implicit-sync path.
rationale: Retrofitting explicit sync later is the exact pain Wayland went through and the native protocol should not repeat it.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the compositor rendering backend policy (Vulkan-only, or Vulkan plus GL fallback) based on the selected target hardware list.
rationale: A single backend reduces maintenance but may exclude older target laptops chosen for V2.

text: Retain Linux AMD, Intel and NVIDIA graphics driver support (DRM) in the forked kernel.
Preserve Linux GPU drivers as the graphics mechanism underneath native Surface/Buffer objects.
Preserve Linux DRM/KMS in the fork initially.
Define Object<Surface>.
A native application must not automatically receive screen contents.
Define the GPU capability that a launched application receives (render/compute queues without other surfaces).
MemoryObject supports the GPU-compatible property (importable by the GPU driver).
A Renderer hands a MemoryObject to the GPU without copying (GPU import of the same physical pages).
The system understands GPU accessibility of a MemoryObject.
Investigate dma-buf interoperability between MemoryObject and the DRM drivers for zero-copy GPU import.
ResourceDomain GPU budget must replace vendor-specific GPU control interfaces for native software.
Investigate whether GPU time and memory budgets can be enforced with current DRM scheduler and cgroup GPU controller support for AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA drivers.
The compositor must be restartable without ending the session.
Selected GPU user-space services must be restartable where driver support permits.
Demonstrate compositor crash → restart → surfaces rebound → applications continue rendering without restart (V0.5 service restart/rebind demo per §60).
Surface and window objects must survive compositor restart (owned by the kernel or a persistent broker) so the restarted compositor can re-attach them.
Define which compositor state (window geometry, stacking order, focus, workspace) is restored after restart and where it is checkpointed.
Where hardware or driver constraints prevent seamless recovery (e.g. GPU reset), the system must report explicit degraded recovery to the user and to clients rather than silently failing.
Run higher-level GPU services (shader compilation, allocation brokers, display management policy) in user space above the retained DRM/KMS kernel drivers (cross-ref GFX).
Retain Linux DRM/KMS as the kernel graphics infrastructure for the initial implementation.
Retain mature Linux GPU drivers (amdgpu, i915/xe, nouveau/NVIDIA) unmodified where possible (§55, §56.1).
Native graphics APIs must not expose DRM ioctls, device nodes or drm_fourcc details directly to applications.
Define and implement the Surface graphics abstraction.
Define and implement the Buffer graphics abstraction as a GPU-compatible MemoryObject (§16).
Define and implement the RenderQueue abstraction.
Define and implement the ComputeQueue abstraction (shared with §37 heterogeneous compute).
Define and implement the Display abstraction including mode, refresh, scaling, HDR and VRR metadata.
Define and implement the Frame abstraction with explicit synchronisation (fences/timelines) for presentation.
Run the compositor as a privileged user-space service component holding Display and DRM master capabilities.
Decide the user-space GPU API native applications render with (Vulkan via Mesa inside the component, a WebGPU-like native API, or both) (ADR).
Resolve how Mesa (which depends on libdrm and Linux device nodes) is used by native components without exposing DRM to the application.
Gate GPU access behind Capability<RenderQueue>/Capability<ComputeQueue> granted at component creation (§9 PhotoEditor example).
Build a new desktop compositor designed around the native object model (Surface, Frame, Display, capabilities).
Compositor must be GPU accelerated.
Compositor must support variable refresh rate.
Compositor must support HDR including a colour management and tone-mapping pipeline.
Compositor must support fractional scaling.
Compositor must be multi-GPU aware (render on one GPU, scan out on another; hybrid laptops).
Compositor must support per-display scaling.
Compositor must support robust crash recovery: on restart, surfaces are rebound and applications continue (§32).
Compositor must support remote surfaces (surfaces whose producer is in a VM or on another machine, §43).
Compositor must implement explicit screen-sharing capabilities granted per surface/display through an OS-owned picker.
Compositor must implement frame scheduling (client frame callbacks aligned to display deadlines).
Compositor must implement latency-aware presentation (present as late as possible before scanout to minimise latency).
Compositor must implement power-aware rendering (skip idle frames, lower refresh on battery, integrate with energy policy §22).
Decide compositor architecture: monolithic display server plus shell, or split display server / window manager / shell components (ADR).
Evaluate reuse of existing compositor infrastructure (Smithay, wlroots, Mutter, KWin) for DRM/KMS plumbing versus building anew, and record in an ADR.
Implement multi-monitor support including hotplug, arrangement and per-display configuration (§62).
Build an automated test that kills the compositor and verifies all client surfaces rebind and continue rendering.
Define window objects (§60) and the window management policy interface between compositor and shell.
Decide whether Wayland is served directly by the native compositor or by a bridge component translating Wayland into the native UI protocol (ADR).
GPU risk assessment: document why GPU drivers are the hardest hardware problem and the mitigation plan for AMD, Intel and NVIDIA.
Preserve Linux DRM/KMS kernel GPU driver infrastructure initially; no native kernel GPU driver rewrite before 1.0.
Prototype how native Surface/Buffer/RenderQueue abstractions map onto DRM/KMS, GBM and Vulkan WSI without exposing DRM file descriptors to native applications (cross-ref §39).
Mesa (Vulkan and OpenGL) userspace running inside native Components with GPU access mediated by Capability<ComputeQueue>/Capability<Surface>.
Do not build a brand-new GPU stack; retain DRM/KMS and Mesa.
Initial native compositor built on the native object model (cross-ref §40).
Window objects: Capability<Surface>/window handles created and managed through typed interfaces.
GPU acceleration for native applications and the compositor.
Multi-monitor support with per-display scaling and arrangement.
HDR output for native applications and compatibility personalities.
Variable refresh rate support.
External displays: hotplug, docking stations, USB-C/DisplayPort Alt Mode.
